newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Labour calls for water industry summit.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Labour calls for water industry summit.

text.p: Britain's opposition Labour Party launched a fierce attack on the water industry on Thursday and said it would call an industry summit if it won power in the election on May 1 to "thrash out what needs to be done".

In a statement to mark the launch of a report entitled "A better water industry", Labour's environment spokesman Frank Dobson said the summit would bring together water companies, regulators, environmental and consumer groups.

He said Labour, which is way ahead of the ruling Conservative party in opinion polls, would "set and enforce tough mandatory leakage targets" in an effort to cut the amount of water seeping out of pipes, which it said was over 810 million gallons (3.6 billion litres) a day.
"The country is facing a water crisis...yet the Tory government is doing nothing about it," Dobson said in the statement.

Britain is suffering its worst drought for 200 years and water companies are already warning that non-essential domestic use might have to be curtailed if rainfall remains unseasonally low through to the summer.

In 1995, the hottest summer on record saw many water companies restricting the use of hosepipes and other non-essential water demand, with Yorkshire Water on the brink of introducing cuts in essential domestic supplies.

Labour has been a fierce critic of the industry, which was privatised by the Conservative government in 1990 and has come under attack since for the hefty salaries paid to directors and large shareholder payouts.
Dobson said the Conservatives had "acted as apologists for the water bosses, instead of championing the needs of consumers and the environment".
He said leakage targets set by a potential Labour government would have to be met at no extra cost to customers.
Labour has already vowed to introduce a one-off "windfall" tax on utilities if it wins power which would be used to bring 250,000 young and long-term unemployed back into jobs.

Dobson said in addition to the mandatory leakage targets, Labour would also make water firms provide a free leakage repair programme for domestic users and take a tough line on licences to shift water from reservoirs and boreholes.
It would also require companies to compensate customers for interruptions to domestic supplies, which companies are obliged to do now in certain circumstances.
Dobson said Labour would introduce tougher fines for pollution along with other measures aimed at curbing demand and making data more readily available to the public.

He claimed the regulatory regime for water was "unable properly to carry out its duties", and said the industry had made 11.1 billion pounds ($18 billion) of profits since privatisation while capital investment had been cut by 361 million pounds.

Dobson also said that water companies had paid "virtually no mainstream corporation tax since privatisation" because they were given tax allowances at privatisation on 7.7 billion pounds invested when they were in the state sector.
"Labour wants a world class, water-efficient, sustainable water industry for Britain," Dobson said. ($ = 0.616 British Pounds)
